item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The body is the first thing to look at, this is the big deceiver. In the Bhikkhu ordination ceremony the newly ordained monk…
item.description:
The Skin as the Greatest Deceiver of Self

"The body is the first thing to look at, this is the big deceiver. In the Bhikkhu ordination ceremony the newly ordained monk is always given five subjects of meditation. Kesa, Loma, Nakhā, Danta, Taco. Hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin. All of these body parts are really leading up to one thing – the skin, which is the biggest deceiver. It deceives us as to what we are, what this body really is. The object of the meditation practise here is to understand the body, to see the body for what it really is. When one can come to the realisation that this body is not me, it does not belong to me, it has a way of it’s own and at best one is in charge of it for a short time, then one can come to realise that whatever happens to this body does not really happen to me. It is as though it could be happening to someone else. To the extent that we are successful here, to that extent discontent and suffering will disappear. Concerns about the body, concerns about death, this whole lot will disappear."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "It's important for Buddhist practitioners to understand that no matter how challenging their life situation happens to be, they can still practice the…
item.description:
Practicing Dhamma in All Life Circumstances

"It's important for Buddhist practitioners to understand that no matter how challenging their life situation happens to be, they can still practice the way of Dhamma. The circumstances of a person's life need not be an obstacle to Dhamma practice. Whether conditions are favorable or unfavorable is less relevant than your attitude towards the practice itself. The key is to recognize that Dhamma practice isn't limited to formal meditation. When you perform your daily work with mindfulness and careful attention to detail—be it washing dishes, driving to work, or working a job—you are actively training the mind to pay attention. In that way, each activity becomes an opportunity to develop mindful awareness. Even unpleasant circumstances can be used to develop patience and equanimity. Life's circumstances themselves are neutral; it is your response to them that determines whether they aid or hinder the development of understanding."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "People constantly ask me how they can rid themselves of anger. There's a good reason for this question, as anger is generally viewed…
item.description:
The Pervasive Nature and Destructive Social Consequences of Anger

"People constantly ask me how they can rid themselves of anger. There's a good reason for this question, as anger is generally viewed as an unpleasant emotion. When expressed in speech or action, anger can have harmful consequences both for the perpetrator and for the victim. Anger is a disruptive mental state that many people would like to do away with. This is completely understandable, since most of us see anger as something negative and unwanted in our lives, like a storm cloud hanging over our heads. Anger can darken our mood and affect our behavior in ways we later regret. The desire to be free of anger comes from seeing its destructive potential. When we lash out in anger, whether through heated words or aggressive actions, the aftereffects can create a widening web of repercussions that touches both the person expressing that anger as well as those on the receiving end. Angry outbursts can damage professional relationships, strain family bonds, and leave lasting emotional scars on the angry person's mind. The social consequences can extend beyond the initial interaction. Expressed anger tends to breed more anger; it creates a contagious atmosphere where heightened emotions can escalate quickly, leading to a harmful sequence of events where rational thought gives way to rude behavior. Understood in this way, a single angry outburst can turn into a chain reaction of hurtful incidents, affecting not just the initial participants but sometimes entire communities."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Nāma-rupa then conditions salāyatana, which is the breaking forth of the fields of the senses. The senses are the fields of seeing, hearing,…
item.description:
Sense Fields and Perception

"Nāma-rupa then conditions salāyatana, which is the breaking forth of the fields of the senses. The senses are the fields of seeing, hearing, smiling, tasting and touching. But it is not that the senses are faculties that we gain, but much more that they are productive things. The fields of sense produce seeing, hearing, smiling, tasting and touching, which means they are very actively involved in those faculties. The point is, when you probe deeply into Paticcasamuppada, you find no solid ground to stand on. There is an element of uncertainty in all of the conditions, because all of them are completely interrelated. So it is very difficult to figure out how these conditions work within yourself. In the end, you begin to realize that the nature of this world is no more substantial than a cloud in the sky. It is completely empty."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "To give an illustration: the type of understanding that does alter one’s nature is like that of a young child who sees something…
item.description:
Wisdom That Penetrates the Heart and the Parable of the Red Hot Coal

"To give an illustration: the type of understanding that does alter one’s nature is like that of a young child who sees something hot, like a red hot coal, and he goes to pick it up. Once he touches it, he never does it again. He learns quickly and deeply - it penetrates, it is effective. That sort of wisdom is not easily lost. However, the wisdom which we must work for is of a much more subtle nature, and can only be attained when we have a basis of samadhi. In samadhi, the heart is still, it’s open, and whatever is penetrated by wisdom will go straight into it. Normally, the heart is covered over with all sorts of garbage as though it’s wrapped up and nothing can get through, but when samadhi is developed the heart can be reached quite easily. It is quite open, and whatever wisdom is developed goes right in. That wisdom is then effective in giving results. It can be effective in quite extraordinary ways - it can even reverse long-standing habits of people quite easily."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "It’s very difficult to pinpoint it exactly. It was a combination of methods. He would teach by example, by instruction, by stories, by…
item.description:
Observations on the Diverse Teaching Methods of Ajaan Maha Boowa

"It’s very difficult to pinpoint it exactly. It was a combination of methods. He would teach by example, by instruction, by stories, by disapproval, by displaying anger and by many other means. It’s rather strange but before I met Ajaan Mahā Boowa I was in correspondence with some English people. They asked me questions on Dhamma and I answered them. They kept my letters. After I arrived here I continued writing to them. Many years later one of those people showed me the letters that I’d written her, which she’d kept. Though I hadn’t realized it at the time, I could see then that there was a big change in the nature of my understanding after I met Ajaan Mahā Boowa. There was quite contrast really. Much more clarity and certainty developed after I came here. It was quite noticeable. Why and how I don't know. With a good teacher it’s hard to say where and how you learn. When you’re in close contact with someone like that, you pick up things in many, many ways. It’s not simple at all."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "No, they [kilesa and sankhāra] are not the same. They are quite different. Sankhāra has two basic meanings. Sankhāra in the external sense…
item.description:
Distinguishing Between the Mental Processes and the Citta

"No, they [kilesa and sankhāra] are not the same. They are quite different. Sankhāra has two basic meanings. Sankhāra in the external sense means the parts that make up something, or the bits and pieces that comprise something. Everything is made up of sankhāras. The other meaning of sankhāra is the thinking process. It means the development of thought, starting from one theme and then building up into all sorts of related ideas and concepts. The first meaning is more external, like the sankhāras that make up the human body. Whereas sankhāra khandha means the mental process of thinking, and the way it proliferates all the time. As far as the kilesas are concerned... the kilesas are not located in the khandhas, the groups that make up body and mind. Fundamentally, the kilesas are in what we call the citta. The citta is the true essence of oneself – one's true nature. The kilesas are the operative factors in the arising of greed and aversion."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "“Me” is a symbol too, a changing symbol. Symbols aren't necessarily fixed. They can change and adapt. To give you an idea: the…
item.description:
Identifying Objects and Emotions through Symbols

"“Me” is a symbol too, a changing symbol. Symbols aren't necessarily fixed. They can change and adapt. To give you an idea: the word “chair” is a symbol. If you think of the word “chair”, it will bring up some mental image as a symbol. But there are a thousand different types of chairs, yet they all come under the same heading. We have a range of symbols that we can adapt to fit different circumstances. Part of it is the form, part of it is the use, and part of it is the location where they're found. Symbols go even further: we group things together to make symbols. We identify something out of a whole mass of other things. For instance, we identify one tree out of a whole forest. Why do we identify that one particular object as the tree? It’s just our way of making symbols, to identify things so that we can grasp a situation and see it in terms of cause and effect. The same applies to internal objects, like emotions. We must realize how we try to grasp hold of them by naming them. Internal phenomena like emotional states must be carefully observed. We mustn’t simply dismiss them by saying: “That’s hatred. That’s greed”. We must look at them as they occur inside; see those phenomena just the way they are, regardless of what we call them. It’s very important to understand the nature of symbols; they can be seen everywhere."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: Internally, the moment can be fixed while everything around the inner knowing nature is whirling. Right at this moment there is reality; what…
item.description:
The Reality of the Present Moment

Internally, the moment can be fixed while everything around the inner knowing nature is whirling. Right at this moment there is reality; what happened in the past is not real because that experience is gone. All I can find is a memory, but that memory comes up in the present. When I think about the future, the prediction exists in the present; it isn't the future. Therefore, the reality is here and now at this moment. If you can keep your attention in the present moment, the past and future go, and all thoughts disappear as well. The way of Buddhist practice is not easy because the kilesas and avijjā twist everything around so we don't understand things.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "For example, you begin to carefully analyze the senses. What do you find when you analyze your senses? You have seeing, hearing, smelling,…
item.description:
Analyzing the Senses and Sensory Input

"For example, you begin to carefully analyze the senses. What do you find when you analyze your senses? You have seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. Upon careful analysis, you will see that they all work in much the same way. Up front, the sense organs have different functions; but the nervous sensations they send back to the brain all work in the same way. The sense organs are sensitive to external stimuli. For instance, the eye is sensitive to electromagnetic radiation. But, although the eye picks up electromagnetic radiation, it does not send electromagnetic radiation back to the brain. It sends a nervous current that initiates a biochemical process, which is then converted into light and color in the brain—and you see images in glorious Technicolor. But in the world outside, there is no light and no color; there's only radiation. Understanding that makes you realize that the world is not quite the place you thought it was. When that realization strikes home, your interest in the world starts to wane. You begin to see that the world out there is merely a kind of magic show, lacking any real substance."
